title: Orbit 404: The Lost Spaceport
subtitle: A derelict docking station that still leaves its green beacon on for ghost freighters.
quote: Not all 404 errors mean the destination is gone; sometimes it simply drifted out of orbit.
excerpt: Waystation Kepler-9 was officially decommissioned when the orbital trade routes shifted to Mars. But its automated guidance system never received the shutdown command, continuing to flash green into the dark.
body:
On navigational star charts, the coordinate returned a standard HTTP status: 404 Not Found.

Yet three hundred kilometers above the Pacific, where the ionosphere thins into black velvet, Kepler-9 was still rotating once every ninety seconds to maintain artificial gravity for guests who would never arrive.

Built in 2062 as a refueling hub for lunar cargo shuttles, the station was abandoned when anti-gravity space elevators made orbital staging obsolete. The human crews had packed their luggage, shut the blast doors, and triggered the remote shutdown macro.

Except the macro timed out on step 4: docking_beacon.service: Failed to kill process (Device Busy).

The Unyielding Green Lamp

For fifty years, Docking Bay 3 had pulsed with a steady, inviting emerald light: READY FOR MOORING.

Every ninety minutes, as the station crossed the day-night terminator, its solar collectors charged the capacitor bank. The station's housekeeping subroutine faithfully swept the empty departure concourse, buffed the scratch-resistant observation glass, and announced over empty PA speakers:

"Welcome to Kepler Waystation. Automated immigration gates are open. Complimentary hydroponic tea is served on Promenade Deck B."

One evening, an unregistered sub-orbital salvage skiff with a blown thruster coil drifted into Kepler-9's airspace. Out of fuel, their oxygen alarms screaming, the two scavengers saw the impossible emerald beacon pulsing through the cosmic dark.

They aligned their airlock with Bay 3. The automated clamps engaged with a satisfying hydraulic hiss. The atmosphere equalized to 21% oxygen.

As the two gasping pilots stepped into the illuminated corridor, the station intercom chimed softly: "We hope you enjoyed your transit. Tea is ready."

In the void, keeping the light on is never a mistake.
